title: Microsoft well positioned to weather AI slowdown, says Jefferies after Ignite meetings - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) is well positioned to withstand a potential slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) spending and gain market share, according to Jefferies, which emerged more positive after meetings with management and customers at the company's Ignite conference. The brokerage said Microsoft's broad software and cloud platform, financial strength and growing use of internally developed AI models and custom silicon should help it manage industry volatility and improve returns on investment. Jefferies highlighted the company's focus on efficiency rather than simply expanding computing capacity, with management citing potential cost savings of 40% to 60% from custom silicon compared with third-party solutions. Software optimisation and dynamic workload allocation are also helping improve infrastructure utilisation, supporting profitability as AI investment increases. Microsoft's cloud business faces constraints involving power, CPUs, memory, storage and skilled labour, but management is prioritising investment while protecting long-term returns. Jefferies said Azure's second-quarter constant-currency growth guidance of 49% to 50% reflected capacity allocation decisions as well as physical infrastructure bottlenecks. The brokerage also sees AI agents creating further opportunities for Azure, as automated systems could consume substantially more database, storage, analytics and CPU resources than individual human users. Customer feedback on Microsoft's Copilot and Cowork offerings was more positive at Ignite, with improvements in context and user experience, although enterprise adoption remains at an early stage. Jefferies said potentially high consumption costs could slow initial deployment but create opportunities for longer-term revenue per customer growth. The brokerage described Microsoft's valuation as attractive at 24 times forward earnings, below its 10-year average of 28 times, against forecast financial year 2027 revenue growth of 20%. title: Intel Jumps on Foundry Win, Anthropic IPO & MSFT Deal - TradingPedia
content: Intel Corporation shares advanced 4.6% in pre-open trading after CEO Lip-Bu Tan announced at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas on Wednesday evening that the company had landed its first external customer for its advanced 18A chip manufacturing technology. The agreement marks a key step in Intel’s strategy to position itself as a serious player in contract chip manufacturing. The name of the customer was not revealed. However, Intel’s technology chief Pushkar Ranade specified that the deal covers the 18A-P manufacturing node, which entered risk production in June 2026. Intel’s pre-market strength was also supported by enthusiasm around Anthropic’s initial public offering. The AI company priced its shares at $83, above the $70-78 range it had marketed. The offering raised $81.3 billion and implied a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, described as the largest IPO on record. The scale and pricing of the IPO helped restore confidence in AI-related capital spending and sparked broad-based pre-market gains across semiconductor and hardware stocks. Momentum for Intel was further reinforced by an expanded long-term collaboration with Microsoft focused on Azure cloud and AI infrastructure. Under the updated partnership, Microsoft will become the first company to deploy Intel Foundry’s EMIB advanced packaging technology for its own Azure silicon. The companies also confirmed a multi-year supply agreement for Intel’s next-generation Xeon server processors, underscoring Intel’s importance within Microsoft’s data center and AI roadmap. Intel continued to execute on its restructuring agenda by launching another round of layoffs this week, targeting its global IT organization. The move contributed to investor confidence that CEO Lip-Bu Tan is maintaining a firm focus on cost control, a stance that markets have generally interpreted positively. The broader trading environment has been favorable to Intel’s move. U.S. equity futures pointed higher in pre-market activity, with the Nasdaq-100 leading the advance. Within technology and semiconductors, sentiment has been lifted by anticipation around Anthropic’s first day of trading on the Nasdaq and reduced anxiety over AI spending following strong results from sector peers earlier in the week. During today’s session, the S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq indices were all trading in positive territory. Collectively, the new 18A foundry customer win, the strengthened Microsoft relationship, and the constructive macro and market backdrop have driven a sharp pre-market rise in Intel shares. The move offers a near-term boost for a stock that remains about 60% below its 52-week high of $142.35, as market participants continue to balance Intel’s longer-term turnaround efforts against ongoing challenges in PC demand and margin pressure. He described the failure as a rare combination of conditions: a hidden bug that sat in the system until a particular traffic pattern triggered it. Microsoft has run an incident response and says it will act on the architectural and operational lessons. That is a statement of intent that came with no timeline and no budget. He also said it should have built bulkheads, which are internal barriers that stop a local failure from spreading across the whole system, so the problem never became a global outage. The Zhitong Finance APP learned that Morgan Stanley released a research report, reiterating its "Overweight" rating on Microsoft (MSFT.US) with a price target of $650. The Morgan Stanley analyst team led by Adam Wood stated that after Microsoft held its Ignite conference in San Francisco and interacted with CEO Nadella and CFO Amy Hood, the firm believes Microsoft is one of the few software companies that have already realized returns on their AI investments. Computing Power Strategy: Avoid blindly maximizing long-term GPU contracts; maintain diversified computing power service offerings. In its report, Morgan Stanley noted that, in allocating computing resources, Microsoft's management treats GPUs as modular assets and refrains from blindly pursuing long-term GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) contracts. Management stated that the company will proactively reserve computing capacity to serve its own first-party products, the Foundry platform, and external enterprise customers, rather than locking all resources into long-term agreements. From Microsoft's perspective, model labs are merely key clients and do not represent the entirety of its cloud business; maintaining elastic computing capacity is a proactive investment in the value of its own platforms and applications, aimed at capturing monetization opportunities for high-value-added services built on top of its infrastructure. Regarding the market's attention to the Neocloud architecture strategy, Microsoft stated that its underlying strategy has not changed; the priority remains building its own data centers, followed by a long-term leasing model in which Microsoft controls data center fit-out, networking, and hardware equipment. This approach allows for better management of data center operational efficiency, deployment pace, and capital expenditures on equipment. The cancellation of some third-party partnership orders stems from suppliers' inadequate service performance, rather than a shift in Microsoft's overall computing power procurement strategy, nor does it signify a major change in the market's computing power supply-and-demand dynamics. Meanwhile, Microsoft's improvements in computing efficiency are not limited to the GPU level; CPU utilization and the storage system are also key focuses of optimization. Moreover, the newly deployed infrastructure inherits this optimization strategy, so the efficiency gains are not confined to existing server clusters. However, the bank cautions that efficiency gains should not be treated as an independent upward variable in computing capacity planning; rather, efficiency improvements can simultaneously boost revenue-carrying capacity and reduce delivery costs. Profitability and Gross Margin: Improvements at the product level take precedence, while the cloud business mix will temporarily weigh on the overall gross margin. Morgan Stanley specifically pointed out a key point that is easily confused by the market: Microsoft's management team's core objective is to improve the gross margins of Azure and M365 individually; the overall gross margin for Microsoft Cloud disclosed in the financial report is merely a result of business development, not a direct performance metric for management. Even if the profitability of individual products continues to improve, once the proportion of the high-growth but relatively low-margin Azure business keeps expanding, it will still dilute Microsoft's cloud consolidated gross margin. Investors should not simply conclude that the profitability of individual cloud services is weakening just because the overall gross margin is under pressure. When assessing future profit improvements, the focus should be on tracking resource utilization, infrastructure efficiency, model operating costs, and the consumption scale of high-value platform services. Enterprise AI Flywheel: Positioned as a multi-model orchestration layer, it is not limited to in-house large models; Microsoft IQ closes the capability loop. Microsoft does not bet its competitiveness on a single model; the core value for enterprise customers lies in the entire ecosystem surrounding the model: enterprise business context, model scheduling framework, memory capabilities, and secure, trustworthy governance. Enterprises can mix cutting-edge large models, Microsoft's self-developed specialized MAI models, and open-source weight models. The Microsoft platform is responsible for selecting the most cost-effective model based on task requirements to get the job done, while keeping control of enterprise business data with the customer and providing unified management of the security, permissions, and cost expenditures of all AI agents. At this conference, Microsoft IQ was unveiled, integrating Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ, further connecting the entire enterprise AI flywheel and tightly coupling business data, model orchestration, and application distribution. Morgan Stanley believes that the more models available on the market, the higher the strategic value of Microsoft as a platform layer that bridges models and enterprise business workflows. Copilot Commercialization: Dual-Drive Model of Subscriptions and Pay-as-You-Go, with Early Adoption in Non-Code Scenarios Microsoft has adopted a hybrid business model that combines subscription-based pricing with usage-based billing: subscriptions provide stable base revenue, while usage-based billing generates incremental income in line with customers' actual AI workloads. Management disclosed that some large customers have already spent more on the Copilot Cowork product than on Microsoft's other products combined; however, the CFO team emphasized that this case is an extreme outlier and not representative of the broader customer base. Moreover, the product suite has only recently been commercialized, so it is still too early to establish reliable expectations for adoption rates. Currently, Copilot's adoption in coding-related workflows is strong, but consumer use across broader knowledge‑work scenarios remains in the early stages of development. While growth potential is significant, the pace of real‑world deployment remains a key uncertainty. Drawing an analogy to Azure's early development, management notes that as enterprises embrace AI agents, their demand for cost control and transparent spending is particularly pronounced. Microsoft has launched Agent 365, a business analytics and cost-management tool that ties AI expenditures to operational outcomes and budgetary alerts, helping companies manage fluctuating AI usage and remove barriers to large-scale deployment. However, the direct revenue generated by this suite of tools depends on the pace at which enterprises expand production-grade AI workloads. In-house chip strategy: Maia and Cobalt serve as efficiency supplements; not all workloads are migrated to in-house hardware. Microsoft's custom chips are part of a diversified computing fleet and do not aim to migrate all workloads to in-house hardware. Take the Maia AI chip and the newly released Cobalt 200 as examples: the Cobalt 200 targets agent-based AI workloads, delivering up to 50% better performance than its predecessor, the Cobalt 100. Microsoft will continue to procure chips from external vendors; the goal of its in-house chips is to enhance performance and reduce costs in specific scenarios, serving as a complementary lever for overall computing efficiency rather than an exclusive replacement. This approach continues the earlier trend of diversifying computing chips from a single source—Intel (INTC.US)—to include AMD (AMD.US) and Cobalt. Sourcing components, securing power, constructing campuses on schedule and bringing capacity online efficiently all bear on how smoothly demand is met, and the market watches those details closely because they shape how quickly the company can convert surging interest into live services. Capital discipline is the other side of the ledger. Keeping that balance steady is central to how the model performs through the current cycle, and it is a thread traders return to whenever the scale of AI spending is debated. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Patched A Record 1,400 Security Flaws In A Single Month As A "Vullpocalypse" Grips Critical Digital Infrastructure - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 18, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A staggering jump in software vulnerability fixes is reframing how analysts and everyday users understand the wave of technology disruptions hitting major institutions. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) issued patches addressing roughly 1,400 security flaws during a single monthly update, a figure that dwarfs the 170 fixes recorded in the same period a year earlier. The Wall Street Journal reported the record-breaking numbers, which analysts on Yahoo Finance’s “The 8:30” cited as a key data point in understanding the current disruption environment. The outages have touched a broad range of institutions, including Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), and the National Security Agency, alongside Microsoft itself. Hosts Julie Hyman, Pras Subramanian, and Jake Conley discussed how artificial intelligence is now surfacing software exploits at a pace that far outstrips traditional patching cycles, forcing developers to push fixes faster than systems can absorb them. The theory gaining traction among technology professionals is that decades of layered software, built upon older code that engineers no longer fully understand, is fracturing under the pressure of rapid remediation efforts. The phenomenon has been informally dubbed a “Vullpocalypse,” a portmanteau of “vulnerability” and “apocalypse,” capturing the sheer scale of simultaneous security fixes cascading through interconnected systems. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, questioned about the outages while in the Philippines ahead of the Trilateral Summit, pushed back firmly against any suggestion of a coordinated attack or systemic link between the incidents. Rubio stated, “The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated from one another,” adding there was “zero evidence that everything’s connected.” Beyond the technical debate, panelist Jake Conley identified a growing sentiment problem, noting that disruptions are no longer abstract concerns confined to cybersecurity professionals. When ordinary consumers cannot access their bank accounts or face repeated software update prompts across their devices, public anxiety rises in ways that governments and technology companies will be forced to address. The broader backdrop, as Conley observed, is that society is now more deeply embedded in these digital systems than at any previous point, meaning the consequences of instability ripple further and faster than ever before. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

In a slew of releases and updates at its annual Ignite conference, the vendor made it clear it wants to build unity across cloud infrastructure, chips and models to support AI capabilities and accelerate legacy technology modernization — and Azure is a critical component. The hyperscaler expanded Azure's core AI capabilities and built a new, connected path linking its enterprise AI platform Microsoft Foundry to its Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for AI workload choice. It also launched Azure Catalyst, a platform that uses agents to discover applications, map dependencies, provide cost comparisons and generate migration waves, on Tuesday. Microsoft spent years reengineering Azure to support AI demands, Jeremy Winter, corporate VP and chief product officer of the Azure Platform, wrote in a blog post. "That work has forged Azure into a single, co-engineered system, with models, silicon and cloud infrastructure tuned as one and value compounding at every layer." Hypersalers are rapidly building out entire ecosystems to support AI and earn enterprise spend. Hyperscalers, in particular, are diversifying the AI capabilities they provide and support, which includes developing custom-built chips for their cloud platforms. Last month, Microsoft said it plans to make its Azure Maia chips, a family of application-specific integrated circuits, the primary inference system for its products and services. The company is aiming for its Maia 200 chip to support Microsoft Foundry workloads by the end of 2026. At Ignite, Microsoft announced general availability of its custom-designed processors, Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines, built to deliver up to 50% better CPU performance compared with Cobalt 100 VMs. The company also touted new capabilities for building and deploying agents, including the introduction of Microsoft IQ, an enterprise context management platform, for providing critical business context to agents. Google has developed its own tensor processing units and launched a joint venture with Blackstone to provide compute as a service to enterprises. This release demonstrates that Microsoft can develop competitive in-house technology and also shows its plan to compete aggressively on price. On Tuesday, at the Ignite conference in San Francisco, Microsoft unveiled six new AI models covering coding, cybersecurity, image generation, and speech. MAI Code 2: Microsoft claims its coding model achieves 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost; it also reaches 96% of Anthropic Claude Opus's performance while costing only 5% as much. This flagship coding model is designed to handle complex, time-consuming programming tasks, working across multiple files and understanding entire software projects. MAI Code 2 Flash: a smaller, faster model. Microsoft says its performance matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the latter's price; it matches Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the latter's cost. MAI Cyber 2 Flash: a cybersecurity model. Microsoft claims it outperformed GPT-6 Astra on a certain security benchmark, with a cost per task less than 2% of the latter's. Microsoft also plans to offer network-specific models to a limited customer base to help address the surge in software vulnerabilities increasingly exposed by AI tools. Other models: According to Microsoft, MAI Image 2.7 ranks first in image editing; the new transcription and real-time speech models aim to challenge leading competitors. Strategy: Leverage specialized models to gain a cost advantage Cost pressures on enterprise customers are a key backdrop to this launch. Suleiman said he keeps hearing businesses complain that "token spending is skyrocketing." He added, "Our commitment is to deliver the best price-performance ratio in the market, enabling you to truly scale your inference workloads; we also understand that you want models that are truly yours." Microsoft's strategy is to build specialized models for specific tasks, thereby achieving comparable performance at a significantly lower cost. But this strategy involves a trade-off: models optimized for everyday coding tasks won't perform as well in advanced mathematics or scientific research. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella emphasized that the new AI models cover scenarios such as coding, cybersecurity, and decision-making. He also highlighted Copilot Fusion, stating that it can orchestrate multiple models to deliver cutting-edge results at a significantly lower cost. title: Microsoft Stock MSFT Drops Below $500 as Cybersecurity Concerns Hit Tech Stocks - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft (MSFT) stock dipped below $500 but returned above again as technology-sector selling intensifies following recent service disruptions, reports of a U.S. National Security Agency communications outage and growing concerns about infrastructure spending, Anthropic competition and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft shares have extended their retreat from record highs near $560 in early November, falling below $500 as technology stocks face another wave of selling pressure. The stock had recovered sharply following the U.S. midterm elections, but renewed concerns about cybersecurity, operational reliability, competition and infrastructure spending have weakened sentiment. The latest decline comes amid a broader flight to safety, as reports of technology disruptions and potential cybersecurity issues raise uncertainty across financial markets. Reports that the U.S. National Security Agency’s internal communications network is down have added to investor concerns. Reuters, citing CNN, reported that the scope of the disruption was being investigated, with no immediate evidence of a cyberattack. The reports follow technology-related disruptions involving airlines and banks on Thursday and Monday, raising questions about the reliability of critical digital infrastructure. There have also been reports circulating about possible Gmail and Microsoft Outlook disruptions, although another widespread outage has not been confirmed. Google’s status dashboard currently lists no incidents. The market reaction reflects growing sensitivity to operational and cybersecurity risks, with investors reducing exposure to technology stocks and moving toward safer assets. Last week’s disruption affecting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365 adds another source of uncertainty for the software giant. Users reported difficulties accessing email, workplace collaboration tools and cloud-based applications, with Microsoft warning that connectivity problems could affect customers across multiple regions. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at 1:27 p.m. ET, alongside over 46,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 concerning Teams. These figures represent user-submitted reports rather than confirmed numbers of affected customers. Although Microsoft initially reported resolving a Teams disruption affecting North American users, wider connectivity issues subsequently raised concerns about Microsoft 365 customers internationally. Temporary disruptions do not necessarily indicate structural problems, but they highlight how dependent businesses have become on Microsoft’s cloud-based productivity ecosystem. Operational reliability is not the only issue weighing on Microsoft. Investors are increasingly questioning the financial returns from its aggressive infrastructure expansion. Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that Microsoft would finance its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. The commitment builds on a January 2026 pledge to cover electricity costs and grid upgrades rather than transferring those expenses to local residents. Although this approach could reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it reinforces the financial burden of expanding Azure and computing capacity. Investors increasingly want evidence that additional infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue without weakening operating margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $500 today. Competition is another emerging concern following Anthropic’s introduction of workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. Its products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Anthropic also plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central workplace interface. The competitive implications are significant given Microsoft’s reliance on its productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue, increasing approximately 17% year over year and accounting for around 30% of total company revenue. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year over year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, while revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year. However, strong earnings have not eliminated concerns about the capital required to maintain growth. Microsoft also faces at least $44.9 billion in commitments involving Anthropic through June 2033, according to an amended filing. Its Maia 300 custom processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Although custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers, development and deployment require additional investment. Microsoft’s retreat below $500 weakens its recovery and leaves the stock exposed to further selling if technology-sector risk aversion continues. The combination of cybersecurity concerns, service disruptions, Anthropic competition and rising infrastructure costs is creating additional pressure on investor sentiment. Despite strong earnings and cloud growth, shareholders increasingly want evidence that Microsoft’s enormous capital commitments can translate into sustainable returns and stronger free cash flow.

Ignite is more focused on enterprise customers, and Microsoft will use it to showcase its latest advancements in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data, security, and intelligent agents. Zhitong Finance APP learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US)'s annual Ignite conference will be held in San Francisco, USA, from November 17 to 20. Unlike the Build conference, which focuses on showcasing software development tools and new technologies for developers, Ignite is more geared toward enterprise customers, and Microsoft will use it to highlight its latest advancements in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data, security, and intelligent agents. Morgan Stanley views this year's Ignite as a key milestone for assessing the progress of Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy, rather than merely a new-product launch event. The firm maintains an "Overweight" rating on Microsoft with a price target of $650. Morgan Stanley's core conviction is that Microsoft is building an "enterprise AI flywheel" comprising Azure, Fabric, Foundry, and Microsoft 365 Copilot: Azure provides underlying computing power, Fabric integrates enterprise data and business context, Foundry helps customers select and orchestrate models and build agents, and Copilot embeds AI capabilities into employees' daily workflows. In Morgan Stanley's view, what truly deserves attention at this conference is not how many new features Microsoft unveils, but whether this technological ecosystem can be translated into more enterprise production deployments, higher product consumption, and more sustainable revenue growth. Key event schedule: Nadella's keynote speech will be held in the early hours of the 18th, Beijing time. According to the official Ignite schedule released by Microsoft, the conference will be held at the Moscone Center in San Francisco from November 17 to 20, with online events also available. The opening keynote will take place at the Chase Center in San Francisco and will be co-hosted by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Judson Althoff. In addition, the Morgan Stanley report also lists the investor communication schedule with Microsoft's management: on November 17 at 4:00 PM Eastern Time, a session with Nadella will be held; on November 18 at 3:00 PM Eastern Time, there will be a meeting with Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood and Vice President of Investor Relations Jonathan Neilson. The above are the investor activities listed in the report and are not public keynote speeches. The enterprise AI flywheel is already backed by demonstrated results, but the key lies in whether it can continue to deliver on its promise. Morgan Stanley's optimistic assessment of Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy is primarily based on its latest quarterly results. Microsoft announced its fiscal first-quarter results for 2027 on October 28. For the quarter ended September 30, the company reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year; operating profit increased 21% year over year, with an operating margin of approximately 50%. Azure revenue grew 48% year over year, and Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 18% at constant currency. Commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year. About 30% of this is expected to be recognized as revenue within the next 12 months. This substantial order backlog provides strong visibility into Microsoft's future cloud business growth. Notably, Azure's growth is not solely driven by demand for AI infrastructure. Microsoft management stated that Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, and increased computing power from improved GPU cluster efficiency, along with better CPU resource utilization, jointly fueled Azure's growth. Meanwhile, Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year, or 31% at constant currency. Morgan Stanley believes that Microsoft's advantage lies in its ability to integrate cloud infrastructure, data platforms, model services, and office applications, enabling enterprises to complete multiple stages—from data governance to agent deployment—within the same ecosystem. However, whether this model can truly form a closed-loop business remains to be seen and will require further evidence at this year's Ignite conference. Five Key Highlights: Copilot Monetization, Foundry Orchestration, and Compute Efficiency I. Copilot Commercialization: Shifting from Seat Growth to ARPU Enhancement Whether Copilot can further increase average revenue per user (ARPU) is one of the most important points to watch at this year's conference. Morgan Stanley believes that Microsoft's commercialization strategy is expanding from simply selling Copilot seats to three avenues: increasing the penetration of paid seats, encouraging customers to upgrade to the higher-tier Microsoft 365 E7 plan, and generating additional revenue through a usage-based billing model for agent-driven tasks. During its latest quarterly earnings call, Microsoft disclosed that Copilot's daily active users increased by nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter and more than quintupled year-over-year; the number of customers actively using pay-as-you-go Copilot Credits grew by over 75% quarter-over-quarter. Additionally, the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased by more than eightfold year-over-year. This means Microsoft is trying to expand its AI business model from traditional software subscriptions to charging based on actual usage. As agents take on more workflows, corporate spending is expected to no longer be limited to the IT department's software procurement budget, but will gradually extend to the operating budgets of business units. However, Microsoft also changed the way it discloses Copilot business data in its latest fiscal quarter. The company had previously reported the number of paid seats consecutively and disclosed in July 2026 that Microsoft 365 Copilot had more than 30 million paid seats; but in the latest fiscal quarter, Microsoft did not update this figure, instead emphasizing daily active users, customer usage, and revenue momentum. Chief Financial Officer Hu De stated clearly on the earnings call that the company did not provide an update on Copilot seat numbers this quarter. Although usage metrics have increased, without the latest base figure for paid seats, it remains difficult to accurately assess to what extent the rise in user activity has translated into additional paid revenue. The shift in pricing models is also worth noting. Microsoft has launched the Microsoft 365 E7 plan at $99 per user per month, integrating products such as Microsoft 365 E5, Copilot, Agent 365, and Entra. Meanwhile, Microsoft plans to enable usage-based billing by default for newly purchased Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses sold through its cloud solution provider channel, setting a default quota of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month. This arrangement has been adjusted to roll out gradually starting in the third quarter of fiscal year 2027, from January to March 2027. Therefore, the key question this year's Ignite needs to answer is: Can Microsoft prove that Copilot not only has more active users but can also continuously increase revenue through seat upgrades and pay-as-you-go pricing? II. Foundry: In the era of multiple models, can Microsoft control the agent orchestration entry point? If Copilot is responsible for delivering AI to end users, then Microsoft Foundry serves as the platform for developing and deploying enterprise AI applications. Microsoft said in its latest fiscal quarter that the number of Foundry customers has exceeded 120,000, with related revenue more than tripling year over year; the number of customers using multiple models to build agent solutions has increased fivefold year over year, while revenue from open-source models on Foundry has grown tenfold. Morgan Stanley believes that the growing diversity of model choices may not diminish Microsoft's platform value. On the contrary, as companies need to select among different models and adjust task allocation based on quality, cost, and response speed, a unified model management and orchestration platform could become even more important. During its earnings call, Microsoft also stated that 90% of Copilot queries use Auto mode, with the system dynamically routing between different models to balance quality, speed, and cost. This also reflects Microsoft's efforts to integrate multi-model scheduling capabilities into its own product ecosystem. What's worth watching at this year's Ignite is whether Microsoft can further showcase Foundry's actual progress in model selection, agent development, deployment, and operational management, and whether these capabilities can bring more enterprise workloads and cloud service consumption. III. Fabric: Can Enterprise Data Become a Differentiating Advantage in the AI Era? As the capabilities of foundation models become increasingly widespread, a company's true competitive advantage may increasingly hinge on its ability to enable AI to understand its own business data and workflows. Microsoft Fabric is a key component of this strategy. The platform aims to integrate enterprise data and provide intelligent agents with callable business information and context. Microsoft disclosed in its latest fiscal quarter that it has more than 44,000 paid Fabric customers, up over 50% year over year; meanwhile, more than 19,000 customers are using both Fabric and Foundry. This means that an increasing number of enterprises are beginning to integrate data platforms with AI application development platforms. Morgan Stanley believes that well-governed enterprise data and business context are key advantages that set Microsoft apart from mere model providers. If enterprises are willing to migrate more data and workflows to the Microsoft platform, the synergy between Fabric and Foundry could further drive growth in Azure consumption. IV. The widespread adoption of intelligent agents is driving demand for security; Agent 365 and corporate governance deserve attention. As AI agents evolve from answering questions to performing tasks across applications, managing their access permissions to enterprise data, tool invocations, and operational actions will become increasingly critical. Microsoft is integrating identity authentication, access control, behavior monitoring, and data protection capabilities into its agent management system. Products such as Entra, Defender, and Purview are expected to see increased enterprise demand as a result, while Agent 365 assumes the role of managing, monitoring, and governing AI agents. Microsoft had previously included Agent 365 in the Microsoft 365 E7 plan. During the latest earnings call, Nadella stated that the number of agents registered with Agent 365 has exceeded 50 million, an increase of over 30% quarter-over-quarter. For Microsoft, the growth in the number of agents not only signifies potential cloud computing demand but also indicates that enterprises need new security and governance tools. If Microsoft can integrate agent management with its existing enterprise security products, it could further encourage customers to upgrade to higher-priced enterprise software plans. V. Maia 300: Can a Proprietary Chip Reduce AI Infrastructure Costs? AI computing power demand continues to grow, and data center construction and chip procurement are also putting huge capital expenditure pressure on Microsoft. Therefore, whether self-developed chips can reduce the cost per unit of computing power is a key factor affecting Microsoft's long-term profitability. Microsoft announced its next-generation, in-house AI inference chip, Maia 300, in October and plans to scale up deployment of the Azure Maia series chips starting in 2027. The company expects that Maia 300 will deliver approximately 40% more tokens per megawatt than the previous generation, with rack-level system token throughput up to seven times that of Maia 200. However, improvements in chip performance do not necessarily translate into an immediate reduction in overall costs. Investors should continue to monitor the pace of real-world deployment, the workloads supported, and the cost and efficiency advantages relative to third-party GPU solutions. Morgan Stanley believes that as Microsoft expands its deployment of self-developed chips, improved AI infrastructure efficiency is expected to ease margin pressure and enhance the long-term returns of the Azure business. Gross margins are under pressure, but can operating leverage offset cost pressures? On the flip side of Microsoft's AI business's rapid growth is the continued rise in capital expenditures and infrastructure costs. Microsoft's capital expenditures for the first fiscal quarter reached $45.2 billion, with about three-quarters allocated to short-term assets such as CPUs, GPUs, memory, and storage. The company expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter and projects approximately $170 billion in capital expenditures for the 2026 calendar year. During the same period, the company's free cash flow was $18.6 billion. Microsoft stated that it expects to maintain positive free cash flow in fiscal year 2027, but also noted that it will continue to flexibly utilize financing channels in the future based on the cost of capital and market conditions. Morgan Stanley's model indicates that Microsoft's gross margin may gradually decline from 67.9% in fiscal year 2026 to 65.9% in fiscal year 2027, 64.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 63.5% in fiscal year 2029. However, the firm expects operating margins to remain broadly stable at 46.8%, 46.6%, 46.7%, and 47.2% over the same period, respectively. This means that Morgan Stanley expects Microsoft to offset some of the gross margin pressure from AI infrastructure investments through revenue growth, improved platform efficiency, and cost control. For investors, what truly matters is not whether gross margins decline in the short term, but whether AI investments can generate sufficient revenue and operating leverage to keep operating profit margins resilient. Behind the $650 price target: Valuation hinges on AI commercialization taking hold In terms of valuation, Morgan Stanley maintains a "Overweight" rating on Microsoft and a price target of $650. The firm's base-case scenario is based on fiscal 2028 earnings per share of $24.41, corresponding to a P/E ratio of approximately 26x. Morgan Stanley's bull-case target price is $800, based on fiscal 2028 earnings per share of $27.41 and a P/E multiple of approximately 29; the bear-case target price is $300, corresponding to earnings per share of $22.25. The bank believes that Microsoft is poised to continue expanding its enterprise AI market share through synergy among Azure, Foundry, Fabric, and Copilot. However, this assessment also implies that Microsoft must continually demonstrate that the commercialization progress of its AI products can meet market expectations for growth and profitability. The ultimate test: Can revenue growth keep pace with capital expenditures? Behind this year's Ignite, there are two conditions that must be met simultaneously: on the one hand, after Copilot expands from seat subscriptions to pay-as-you-go pricing, it must genuinely drive revenue growth; on the other hand, Microsoft must improve the utilization of its AI infrastructure to prevent capital expenditures from continuing to rise without a corresponding improvement in return on investment. In the first fiscal quarter, Microsoft's capital expenditures reached $45.2 billion, and they are expected to exceed $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter. Despite strong growth in Azure and Foundry, AI infrastructure investment remains substantial. Microsoft needs to demonstrate to the market that every additional dollar of capital expenditure generates more monetizable computing power and higher revenue returns. Therefore, the most noteworthy developments on Ignite are not any single new model or agent feature, but rather three advancements with greater commercial significance: whether Copilot can boost ARPU through seat upgrades and pay-as-you-go pricing; whether Foundry can become the core platform for enterprise agent deployment in a multi‑model environment; and whether in‑house chips and improved datacenter efficiency can reduce the cost per unit of compute. For Microsoft, the competition in enterprise AI is no longer just about model capabilities; it is also a contest of full-stack commercialization capabilities, spanning from infrastructure to applications and from data to security. Whether Ignite can present a clearer implementation roadmap will become an important window for the market to assess the return on its AI investments.
